sections.html:
The length of notice depends on why the landlord is ending the tenancy. Under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act the shortest period is seven days, and the longest common one is 30 days, for ending a month-to-month tenancy without stating a cause. Notice always comes first, as a written step before any court filing.

SituationNotice required
Unpaid rentWritten notice naming rent and late fees owed; lease ends not less than seven business days after receipt if unpaid
Material lease breach or health and safety violationWritten notice naming the acts; termination date not less than seven business days after receipt
Noncurable default (listed acts)Seven day notice, no right to cure unless the landlord agrees
Week-to-week tenancyWritten notice at least seven days before the termination date
Month-to-month tenancyWritten notice at least 30 days before the periodic rental date

The first three rows come from Section 35-9A-421, subsections (b), (a) and (d). The last two come from Section 35-9A-441, subsections (a) and (b).

sections.h2: What a nonpayment notice must say
sections.html:
It has to be in writing, be delivered to the tenant, and state the rent and any late fees owed. Section 35-9A-421(b) adds that the notice must say the rental agreement will end on a date not less than seven business days after the tenant receives it.

A tenant who pays the full demand inside that period cures the breach, and the lease goes on. If the money does not arrive, the agreement terminates under the statute and the landlord can go to court for possession.

Sometimes one set of facts breaks the lease twice, such as unpaid rent plus a material breach. The statute then makes the seven day nonpayment period control, so the landlord does not run two separate clocks.

sections.h2: Notice for a material lease violation
sections.html:
This is a written notice that lists the acts or omissions making up the breach and sets a termination date at least seven business days after receipt. Section 35-9A-421(a) covers material noncompliance with the rental agreement, an intentional misrepresentation of a material fact in the lease or application, and a failure to meet the tenant's health and safety duties under Section 35-9A-301.

The tenant can fix the problem before the termination date, and an adequate fix keeps the lease alive. One breach cannot be fixed at all: an intentional misrepresentation of a material fact in the rental agreement or application.

Under Section 35-9A-421(c), the landlord may also seek actual damages, reasonable attorney fees and an injunction for the noncompliance.

sections.h2: Violations with no chance to cure
sections.html:
Section 35-9A-421(d) names four kinds of conduct that count as noncurable defaults, and the landlord may end the tenancy on a seven-day notice. The list is described as including, but not limited to, these acts:

  • Making, growing, importing, transporting, possessing, supplying, administering or using illegal drugs in the unit or common areas.
  • Illegal use, manufacture, import, possession, supply or discharge of a firearm or ammunition on the rental property, except in self-defense, defense of another or as allowed by Section 13A-3-23.
  • Criminal assault of a tenant or guest on the property, with the same self-defense exceptions.
  • A second breach with substantially the same acts as one already cured, if it happens within six months.

The same subsection also caps cures in general. A tenant may not cure the breach of any lease term more than two times in a 12 month period unless the landlord consents in writing, regardless of Section 35-9A-141.

sections.h2: Ending a month-to-month or week-to-week tenancy
sections.html:
Use a written notice: 30 days for month-to-month, seven days for week-to-week. Section 35-9A-441 allows either the landlord or the tenant to give it, so a tenant who wants out follows the same periods.

Count the 30 days back from the periodic rental date written in the notice. A landlord who wants the tenant gone by the first of a month should deliver the notice at least 30 days before that date.

This route involves no accusation of wrongdoing. It suits an owner who is selling and simply needs the house empty, and the dates can be lined up with a buyer's closing.

sections.h2: If the tenant stays after the notice ends
sections.html:
The landlord may bring an action for possession. When the holdover is willful and not in good faith, the landlord may recover more: under Section 35-9A-441(c), an amount equal to not more than three months' periodic rent, or actual damages if those are greater, plus reasonable attorney fees.

One counterweight applies. If the landlord consents to the tenant's continued occupancy, Section 35-9A-161(d) governs instead.

Court steps beyond that point, including service, the seven day appeal window and the writ, belong to the eviction lawsuit itself.

A notice cannot be a payback. Section 35-9A-501 bars a landlord from raising rent in a discriminatory way, cutting services, or bringing or threatening an action for possession because the tenant took one of three protected steps:

  • Complaining to a government agency that enforces a building or housing code about a violation materially affecting health and safety.
  • Complaining to the landlord about a failure to maintain the premises under Section 35-9A-204.
  • Organizing or joining a tenants' union or similar group.

A tenant who proves retaliation gets the remedies in Section 35-9A-407 and a defense to the possession case. The landlord can still sue when the tenant is behind on rent, when the tenant or a guest caused the code violation through lack of reasonable care, when repairs would effectively deprive the tenant of the home, or for other material lease violations.

Whatever part of the deposit is unused must go back with an itemized list of what was withheld, within 60 days. Section 35-9A-201 lets the landlord apply the deposit to unpaid rent and to damage from the tenant's failure to meet Section 35-9A-301. The itemized written notice and balance are due 60 days after the tenancy ends and possession is delivered.

A landlord may not demand more than one month's periodic rent as security, except for pets, changes to the premises or increased liability risks. An owner planning a sale should put the 60 day deadline on the calendar.

sections.h2: Does a notice help you sell the house?
sections.html:
A properly served notice gives you a date to plan around, and some buyers will wait for it. Others will not buy until the tenant has left.

We buy Alabama houses in many conditions, including rentals where a notice is out or a case is pending. Send us the address and where you are in the process, and we can talk about a closing date that fits.

faqs.q: How long is an Alabama eviction notice for unpaid rent?
faqs.a: Section 35-9A-421(b) calls for a written notice stating the rent and late fees owed, with termination not less than seven business days after the tenant receives it.

faqs.q: How much notice ends a month-to-month tenancy in Alabama?
faqs.a: At least 30 days, in writing, before the periodic rental date named in the notice, under Section 35-9A-441(b). Landlord or tenant can give it.

faqs.q: Can an Alabama landlord skip the cure period?
faqs.a: For certain acts, yes. Section 35-9A-421(d) lists drug activity, illegal firearm use, criminal assault and a repeat of a cured breach within six months as noncurable, with seven-day termination.

faqs.q: What can a landlord recover from a tenant who stays after the notice?
faqs.a: If the holdover is willful and not in good faith, up to three months' periodic rent or actual damages, whichever is greater, plus reasonable attorney fees under Section 35-9A-441(c).

faqs.q: When does a landlord have to return the deposit in Alabama?
faqs.a: Within 60 days after the tenancy ends and possession is delivered, with an itemized list of any amounts withheld, under Section 35-9A-201.
